name: Displacement of Okhotsk Culture from Northern Hokkaido
summary: Over the 10th–11th centuries the southward-expanding proto-Ainu (late Satsumon) populations displace the Okhotsk culture from northern and eastern Hokkaido. The Okhotsk people, maritime hunter-fishers ultimately related to populations along the lower Amur and the Kuril chain, gradually retreat to Sakhalin and the Kurils, while remnant communities are absorbed into the emerging Ainu world. Archaeological evidence shows the Tobinitai culture, transitional between Okhotsk and Satsumon/Ainu, occupying the Nemuro and Shiretoko peninsulas before the Okhotsk presence in Hokkaido itself disappears.

_quarry.structural_significance: Consolidates Ainu territorial control of Hokkaido and defines the northern and eastern coastlines as Ainu cultural space rather than a contested frontier. The contact also injects Okhotsk technological and ritual elements, particularly bear-cult practices and certain ceremonial assemblages, into Ainu culture, where they persist in iyomante (bear ceremony) into the historic period.
